content.title: Markets News, April 2, 2026: Major Indexes Snap 5-Week Skids as Stocks Rebound from Early Rout; Oil Prices Jump on Iran War Concerns
content.text: Major stock indexes staged a late rally to close the holiday-shortened week mostly higher Thursday even though oil futures soared, as investors mulled the latest Iran developments. The tech-heavy Nasdaq and benchmark S&P 500 finished up 0.2% and 0.1%, respectively, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average ended down 0.1% to snap a three-session winning streak. All three snapped five-week skids, with the Nasdaq, S&P 500, and Dow ending up a respective 4.4%, 3.4%, and 3.0% during the four sessions. While tomorrow is not a federal holiday, the stock market will close in observance of Good Friday, although the Bureau of Labor Statistics is slated to release the March jobs report at 8:30 a.m. ET. The bond market will close early, at 2 p.m. ET. Indexes dropped sharply as markets opened today, briefly got back to near flat on word that Iran was drafting a protocol with Oman to reopen the important Strait of Hormuz shipping channel, then turned lower again before rallying before the close. Yesterday, the indexes began the second quarter by closing sharply higher for a second straight day on cautious optimism the Iran war might end soon. However, in an address to the nation last night, President Donald Trump said that the U.S. would "hit" Iran "extremely hard," adding that "over the next two to three weeks, we're going to bring them back to the Stone Ages where they belong." Oil prices, which have soared since the Middle East fighting began just over a month ago, jumped in response to Trump's comments. West Texas Intermediate crude futures, the U.S. oil benchmark, were up more than 11% to $111.50 a barrel at 4 p.m. ET after hitting nearly $114—their highest level since the conflict started Feb. 28—earlier after Bloomberg said that state-run Iranian news agency IRNA reported that Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said the nation was working with Oman to monitor traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures, the global benchmark, settled up nearly 8% to above $109. Airline and cruise stocks pulled back, as fuel costs are their biggest expense outside of labor. Delta Air Lines (DAL), United Airlines Holdings (UAL), American Airlines Group (AAL), Carnival Corp. (CCL), Royal Caribbean Cruises (RCL), and Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings (NCLH) all were down roughly 1% to 3.5%. Shares of the Magnificent Seven tech giants were mixed, with Tesla (TSLA) leading declines at near 5.5% after it reported worse-than-expected quarterly deliveries. Tesla was the worst-performing stock in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Elsewhere, Globalstar (GSAT) stock surged 13% on a Financial Times report that Amazon (AMZN) was in talks to acquire the satellite communications provider, and Nike (NKE) slipped a further 1% after sinking more than 15% yesterday to lead S&P 500 and Dow decliners. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which affects interest rates on all sorts of consumer loans, reversed earlier gains and slipped below 4.31% from Wednesday's close around 4.32%. The yield had ended last Friday near 4.44%, its highest closing level since last July. Gold futures pulled back 2.5% to $4,695 an ounce. The U.S. Dollar Index, which tracks the value of the greenback against a basket of currencies, was up 0.4% to 100.02. Bitcoin slipped to $67,000 from overnight highs around $68,600. Major Indexes Snap 5-Week Skids April 02, 2026 04:32 PM EDT The three major stock indexes' long weekly losing streaks are over. The tech-heavy Nasdaq, benchmark S&P 500, and blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average snapped five-week skids on this holiday-shortened week, ending up a respective 4.4%, 3.4%, and 3.0% during the four sessions. Stock markets will be closed tomorrow because of Good Friday. Blue Owl's Latest Withdrawal Limits Ratchet Up Investor Concerns About Private Credit April 02, 2026 04:11 PM EDT There's nothing to fear but fear itself...in private credit. Case in point: Blue Owl Capital's private credit woes. Concerns about private credit—that is the $3 trillion market of loans from non-bank lenders such as private funds, asset managers and insurance companies—has driven masses of investors to the exits. In the face of uber high withdrawal requests—for example, Blue Owl's flagship OCIC fund received redemption requests for about 21.9% of shares outstanding in the first quarter, and its tech-focused fund, 40.7% of shares—the firm has further capped redemptions at 5% from 15% previously. Blue Owl stock has lost more than 40% of its value since the start of the year. Michael Nagle / Bloomberg / Getty Images Other asset managers that offer non-publicly traded private credit funds for retail investors—including Apollo Global Management (APO), Ares Management (ARES) and BlackRock (BLK) —recently made similar moves, limiting redemptions as requests accelerated. Private credit experts say the mass withdrawals are effectively stress testing the market, but that the gates on withdrawals don't necessarily indicate something is broken. Read the full article here. -Crystal Kim SBA Communications Stock Leads S&P 500 on Report Tower Operator Mulling Sale April 02, 2026 03:18 PM EDT A report that SBA Communications is mulling selling itself sent its stock soaring Thursday afternoon. SBA Communications (SBAC) shares jumped 14% to lead the S&P 500 in the final hour of trading after Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that the company "is exploring options including a potential sale after the tower owner and operator received preliminary takeover interest." Bloomberg added that the people said that "large infrastructure funds have been circling" SBA, and that "deliberations were at an early stage." With this afternoon's sharp gains, SBA shares moved into positive territory for the year. TradingView Stock Investors Brace for Uncertainty Over the Upcoming Long Weekend April 02, 2026 02:32 PM EDT Investors are heading into the first long weekend since the war in Iran began, and they have reason to be anxious. “Nobody wants to hold risk into the weekend,” Alli McCartney, managing director at UBS Private Wealth Management, told CNBC late last month. The reason, she said, “is anything that happens over the weekend is going to change the flow.” With markets closed tomorrow for Good Friday, the risks of being caught off guard by developments in Iran are even higher this weekend. Stocks were volatile on Thursday as investors tried to parse development in the Middle East. Michael M. Santiago / Getty Images The U.S. has sent thousands of additional troops to the Middle East, a move that investors can’t be sure is a negotiating tactic or preparation for escalation. The U.S. has repeatedly ramped up operations and threats on weekends—the first salvos of the war came late on a Friday night, and President Trump’s threats to target Iran’s energy infrastructure landed on a Saturday. Contradictory messages out of the White House—and Iran’s public denials of nearly everything the Trump administration says—add to the confusion. Read the full article here. -Colin Laidley Overtime Tax Break Draws More Filers Than Expected April 02, 2026 01:50 PM EDT Taxpayers have flocked to one of this year's new tax breaks, according to one government official. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this week that a quarter of taxpayers have deducted their overtime pay so far. That number is more than double the previous estimates of how many taxpayers would claim the new deduction. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a quarter of taxpayers have claimed the new overtime deduction. Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images The "One Big, Beautiful Bill," passed by Congress in July, included several new tax cuts that have so far increased the average tax refund by almost 11%. One of these tax cuts includes the new 'no tax on overtime' deduction. It allows single taxpayers to deduct up to $12,500 of earned overtime wages from their taxable income, reducing their overall tax bill. The IRS did not respond to questions about whether Bessent's comments matched its records. However, a quarter of tax filers claiming the overtime deduction is far above initial estimates of those eligible for the break. -Elizabeth Guevara Inflation Is Changing Americans' Daily Habits—From Thermostat Settings to What's in the Fridge April 02, 2026 01:22 PM EDT One-third of Americans have turned down their thermostat or bought less food, and more belt-tightening may be ahead. More than 85% of consumers said in February that they had made changes to their daily life in response to inflation, according to a survey of 4,000 Americans conducted by JD Power, a consumer insights firm. At that point, inflation was hovering around 2.4% year-over-year. Economists say the conflict with Iran could drive up energy and transportation costs, elevate prices for other goods and increase the broader cost-of-living. Consumers were cutting before the prospect of a war-fueled surge in inflation. Many nixed discretionary purchases, with 45% reducing visits to restaurants or takeout orders, 42% buying less expensive food, and 42% delaying the purchase of apparel, home decor or other items, the survey said. Consumers are turning down the thermostat to cope with inflation, JD Power said. Getty Images Some also started easing off essentials. About 34% of those surveyed turned down the thermostat, and 33% bought less food over the previous 30 days, the survey said. Some 16% of consumers postponed or canceled medical care, or went without medications, the research found. Read the full article here. -Sarina Trangle Deal Talks With Amazon Have This Satellite Internet Provider's Stock Popping April 02, 2026 12:44 PM EDT Amazon could be looking to make a big move to grow its budding satellite internet service. Shares of Globalstar (GSAT) were up over 9% in recent trading following a report the satellite internet company could be acquired by Amazon (AMZN). Talks around a potential deal, which could be worth an estimated $9 billion, are ongoing but could face some hurdles, The Financial Times reported Wednesday. With Thursday's gains, Globalstar shares have climbed more than 20% since the start of the year. Thomas Fuller / SOPA Images / LightRocket / Getty Images One of the complicating factors to clear a deal could include negotiations with Apple (AAPL), which bought a 20% stake in Globalstar in 2024, the report said. Amazon declined to remark, and Globalstar did not immediately respond to an Investopedia request for comment. Read the full article here. -Aaron McDade Acuity Shares Sink on Lowered Lighting Outlook April 02, 2026 12:02 PM EDT Acuity is dealing with a soft lighting market, and its shares are selling off Thursday. Shares of Acuity (AYI) fell nearly 6% in recent trading after the Atlanta-based industrial technology company reported weaker-than-expected fiscal 2026 second-quarter net sales and executives issued a disappointing outlook for its lighting business. Acuity posted Q2 sales of $1.06 billion, up 5% year-over-year but below the Visible Alpha consensus expectation of $1.08 billion. Adjusted earnings of $4.14 per share topped estimates of $4.04 per share. On the company's earnings call, CEO Neil Ashe said that "given our performance year-to-date and our expectations for the lighting market for the remainder of the year, we now expect our full-year [Acuity Brands Lighting] sales performance will be flat to down low-single digits year-over-year." Prior guidance called for ABL sales of up low-single digits. Ashe added that "basically for the first half of the year, ABL is basically down about 1%, and we have really tough comps from all of the order aheads from this time last year." Including today's decline, shares of Acuity Brands are down about 25% thus far in 2026. TradingView Why Complaints About Debt Collection Are Surging April 02, 2026 11:26 AM EDT With significantly higher delinquency and default rates across most loan types, the number of complaints against debt collectors skyrocketed in 2025. There were 471,142 reports against debt collectors in 2025. That is more than double the number of reports submitted in 2024, according to the most recent data from the Federal Trade Commission. Americans can report a debt collector to the FTC if the collector is using "abusive, unfair, or deceptive practices" to collect defaulted credit card, auto, medical, student loan, mortgage, and other household debts. Debt collection complaints spiked after student loan repayments resumed. dusanpetkovic/Getty Images Federal student loan borrowers did not have to make payments during the COVID-19 pandemic payment pause, which ended in October 2023. However, most borrowers did not experience any negative impacts from missing payments until a federal grace period ended in October 2024. Read the full article here. -Elizabeth Guevara The Iran War Is Cutting Off Fertilizer Supplies And Raising Food Prices April 02, 2026 11:12 AM EDT If you thought $4 gasoline was expensive, wait until the Iran War's fertilizer crunch starts showing up on grocery store price tags. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is pushing up more than just gas prices: the blockage of the crucial waterway to ship traffic has cut off about a third of the world's seaborne fertilizer, according to the United Nations. With ships cut off from traveling through Hormuz for more than a month since the war began, fertilizer prices are up nearly 30% in the U.S., according to the Bloomberg Green Markets price index. A tractor drips nitrogen fertilizer onto rows of romaine lettuce at Pisoni Farms near Gonzales, Calif. Nic Coury / Bloomberg via Getty Images "If the conflict doesn't end, and transit reopen allowing those fertilizers to pass through, then we have a lost farming season here in the northern hemisphere, primarily for corn," Kathryn Rooney Vera, Chief Market Strategist at StoneX, said in an interview. "So if we have a lost season, or yields drop because they don't have the inputs that they need, then we should expect food costs to increase." Read the full article here. -Diccon Hyatt Tesla's Sales Struggles Are Improving, But Not as Quickly as Wall Street Hoped April 02, 2026 10:00 AM EDT Tesla's sales struggles improved in the first quarter, though not as much as Wall Street expected them to. Shares of Tesla (TSLA) were down about 4% in recent trading after the company said it delivered 358,023 vehicles in the first quarter, up 6% from the same time a year ago, but short of the 368,900 that analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha called for. Tesla's production of 408,386 vehicles also came in below the 446,060 vehicle analyst consensus. Tesla shares have lost nearly 20% since the start of the year. Justin Sullivan / Getty Images Wedbush analysts said that while deliveries were underwhelming, that was "not a shock to us given the current EV backdrop across geographies while the company shifts gears to focus more on its AI strategy." Read the full article here. -Aaron McDade Apple Turned 50 Years Old. Here's What Its Earliest Investor Saw in the Company and What It Shows About Investing April 02, 2026 09:15 AM EDT Fifty years ago, Apple was born. At its inception, it was little more than two guys—Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak—and a personal computer prototype in a Bay Area garage. It would go on to become one of world's most recognizable brands and largest companies, valued at nearly $4 trillion today. Early investors were instrumental in Apple’s growth from start-up to tech titan. One in particular supplied not just the capital, but also the credibility and business acumen to turn a novel idea—that everyone could own a computer—into a reality. Apple was founded in Los Altos, California, on April 1, 1976. Michael Nagle / Bloomberg via Getty Images Mike Markkula is often described as the adult in the room—the business-minded supervisor who helped channel Jobs’ and Wozniak’s vision. According to Markkula, he backed a $250,000 loan from Bank of America, and told the lender: “I want you hold our feet to the fire.” He insisted the bank treat upstart Apple like a mature, established business. Markkula says that decision helped enforce discipline at a company whose founders cared little for the ins and outs of business. Read the full article here. -Colin Laidley Travel Stocks Sink Amid Fuel Price Concerns April 02, 2026 08:30 AM EDT Several stocks in the airline and cruise industry are falling as the renewed surge in oil prices raises concerns that the companies could face higher fuel costs for longer, pressuring margins. Fuel costs have roughly doubled since the start of the Iran war, and have already led many airlines to raise prices in recent weeks, especially for international flights that require more fuel. Shares of Delta Air Lines (DAL), United Airlines (UAL), American Airlines (AAL) and Southwest Airlines (LUV), along with Carnival (CCL), Royal Caribbean Cruises (RCL) and Norwegian Cruise Line (NCLH), were each down roughly 4% ahead of the opening bell. -Aaron McDade Delta Air Lines was among several travel stocks falling in premarket trading Thursday. Tayfun Coskun / Anadolu via Getty Images SpaceX Filed to Go Public—Here's Every Step Between Now and When You Can Buy Shares April 02, 2026 08:30 AM EDT SpaceX just took its official first step toward a stock market debut that could set records for an initial public offering. Elon Musk's rocket and satellite company reportedly filed confidential paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission Wednesday, with the company looking to raise $40 billion to $80 billion—a figure that would shatter Saudi Aramco's record $29 billion debut in 2020. If SpaceX lists by its July 2026 target, it would be the first of three mega-IPOs this year, along with OpenAI and Anthropic. Patrick T. Fallon / AFP / Getty Images But filing for the IPO is just the first step. Before anyone can buy a single public share, SpaceX has to run a gauntlet that takes most companies up to a year to complete. Read the full article here. -Peter Gratton You Can Save at Least 50¢ on Gas Just Across the Border in 11 States—In Some Cases Over $1 April 02, 2026 07:34 AM EDT With gas prices recently pushed above a $4 national average by the ongoing Iran conflict, differences between states are becoming more noticeable. In some cases, prices can swing by 50 cents or more at the pump over just a few miles. Based on statewide averages, several states currently sit next to much cheaper neighbors—creating potential savings for drivers able and willing to cross the border. Drivers may find noticeably lower gas prices just across a state line, even as the national average tops $4. Scott Olson / Getty Images Many of the largest price gaps show up in Western states—and in some cases exceed $1 per gallon. But savings opportunities appear in parts of the Midwest, South, and Southwest as well. Read the full article here. -Sabrina Karl Inflation Is Rising, And the Fed's Main Tool to Fix It Might Not Work April 02, 2026 07:03 AM EDT The Iran war is causing a surge in energy prices that's likely to stoke inflation in the coming months, and the Federal Reserve's monetary policy playbook may be helpless to stop it. With average gas prices up more than $1 a gallon so far because of the Iran war, economists say other prices are likely to follow suit and lead to a general uptick in inflation. Forecasters at Bank of America, for example, said they expect consumer prices as measured by Personal Consumption Expenditures to rise nearly 4% over the year in the second quarter, up from their pre-war estimate of 3% annual inflation. The Federal Reserve, tasked by Congress with managing inflation, would normally raise its key interest rate to counteract the uptick. But the kind of inflation we're experiencing may not be the type the Fed can control with its monetary policy, according to Fed Chair Jerome Powell and some economists. Jerome Powell and his colleagues at the Fed may have a hard time wrangling supply-side inflation. If Fed officials view their policy as ineffective against the current wave of inflation, they're more likely to hold the central bank's key interest rate steady in the coming months even if prices start rising significantly. The federal funds rate influences borrowing costs on all kinds of loans: raising it tends to discourage spending, while lowering it can promote spending and boost the economy and the job market. TradingView S&P 500 futures pointed 1.3% lower. TradingView Nasdaq 100 futures dropped 1.6%.
